But now we've got a pretty good set of data in hand to say that actually the impacts on core inflation haven't really been that large, with the exception of Australia, where there's good justification as to why we've seen more inflation rise here, because we entered this shock with an excess demand problem for the rest of the world. headline: Rising global term premium spilling into Australian yields given Australia's current account deficit and reliance on global capital markets
reasoning: Dynan notes that Australia is a current account deficit country, meaning it borrows from the rest of the world to fund the gap between domestic savings and investment. As a result, Australian debt is priced in global capital markets and must compete for the same pool of global funds. Any rise in global term premium therefore naturally spills over into Australian term premium and yields. The implication is that Australian bond yields face upward pressure from the same global forces driving US and global long-end rates higher.
quote: It's certainly placing some upward pressure on our yields as well. And and one reason for that is that we are at the end of the day, a current account deficit country. And even though our broader external balance has kind of improved to some degree, we are a current account deficit country. And what that means is that we borrow from the rest of the world to fund our difference between savings and investment. So that means that our debt is going to be set on the global markets as well. And therefore, you know, our our debt is going to price. Price that is we have to compete in that global pool. So any rises in global term premium are naturally going to spill over into inflation term premium.

headline: Bonds losing hedging power against equities in a supply-shock dominated macro environment
reasoning: Dynan notes that bonds have historically served as a hedge against equities in bad economic states, but this property is conditional on the nature of the shock. In demand shocks bonds rally while equities fall, providing portfolio insurance; but in negative supply shocks, both asset classes come under pressure simultaneously. With geopolitical fragmentation increasing the frequency and severity of supply shocks, the insurance value of bonds is diminished, leading investors to demand more compensation — i.e. higher term premium — for holding them.
quote: In negative supply shocks bonds won't be good hedges to equities. So if you think about bonds role in in in macro portfolios I mean one reason historically to have them in your portfolio is that you expect that in bad states of the world, you know, bonds give you some insurance. They should be a hedge against your equities. And that's absolutely true and more true in demand shocks. But in supply shocks, that is less true. Both bonds and equities come under pressure at the same time. So if bonds aren't providing that same insurance property like they used to, they aren't providing it as much. Then investors are going to demand more, um, compensation for that, for that risk going forward.
